title: Cyberpunk 2077 Best Attributes and Perks for Beginners
description: Cyberpunk 2077 beginner attributes and perks explained, including Body, Reflexes, Technical Ability, Intelligence and Cool, plus a flexible early-game progression plan for Update 2.0 and later.
body:
Cyberpunk 2077’s current progression system is much easier to understand once you stop trying to raise every attribute at the same time. Update 2.0 rebuilt the perk trees around fewer, more meaningful abilities, and the best beginner approach is to choose a small number of attributes that support how you actually play.

For most new players, Body and Technical Ability are the safest flexible foundations because they support survivability and cyberware investment. After that, choose one primary direction — mobility, hacking, stealth or another playstyle — instead of spreading points evenly across all five attributes.

For the broader first-playthrough basics, see our [Cyberpunk 2077 beginner’s guide](/stories/cyberpunk-2077-beginners-guide/). If you are still deciding what kind of V you want to role-play before building the character, our [life paths guide](/stories/cyberpunk-2077-life-paths-explained/) explains Corpo, Nomad and Streetkid.
author: Rouane Mounssif
imageAlt: Cyberpunk 2077 promotional artwork used as the feature image for Neural Critic’s beginner attributes and perks guide.

contentBlocks.text:
Cyberpunk 2077 has five core attributes: Body, Reflexes, Technical Ability, Intelligence and Cool. Each attribute opens access to its own perk tree as you invest more points, and those perks are now designed around meaningful abilities rather than tiny percentage increases.

CD Projekt Red’s Update 2.0 also made perks much easier to experiment with. Individual perk points can be refunded for free outside combat, while attributes are a more permanent commitment because the game gives you only a one-time full attribute reset.

That distinction is the most important beginner rule: experiment freely with perks, but spend attribute points with a plan.
contentBlocks.heading: How Attributes and Perks Work After Update 2.0

contentBlocks.text:
Body is the easiest attribute to recommend when you are still learning the game because it supports survivability and physical resilience. The tree includes abilities built around staying active under pressure and improving durability.

A few early Body points give you more room to make mistakes while you learn enemy behavior, cyberware and movement. That value is useful even if Body does not become your main endgame identity.

Beginners do not need to maximize it immediately. Think of Body as a foundation you can invest in until your character stops feeling fragile, then redirect points toward the playstyle you enjoy most.
contentBlocks.heading: Body — The Safest Beginner Investment

contentBlocks.text:
Technical Ability became much more central after Update 2.0 because cyberware is now a core part of character progression. CD Projekt Red moved most armor away from clothing and made cyberware capacity an important limit on how much technology V can install.

The Technical Ability tree supports that system and can improve how much value you get from cyberware-focused progression. That makes it one of the most broadly useful attributes even for players who are not building around a single narrow combat style.

For a flexible first character, pairing some Technical Ability with enough Body to stay comfortable gives you a strong base before specializing.
contentBlocks.heading: Technical Ability — Cyberware Makes This More Valuable Than It Looks

contentBlocks.text:
Reflexes is built around mobility and fast repositioning. Its perk tree can unlock movement abilities that make navigating fights and the open world feel dramatically more fluid.

CD Projekt Red’s own post-2.0 build guidance highlights Dash as an important early Reflexes unlock, which shows how strongly the attribute changes the way V moves rather than simply adding passive numbers.

Choose Reflexes as a major investment if movement, quick repositioning and an active combat rhythm are what you enjoy most. If you prefer hacking or slower stealth, it can remain a secondary attribute instead.
contentBlocks.heading: Reflexes — Best If Movement Is Central to Your Playstyle

contentBlocks.text:
Intelligence is the main progression path for players who want hacking to define their character. Update 2.0 rebuilt netrunning around new perk interactions, including Overclock and more deliberate quickhack management.

This is the attribute to prioritize when you want digital tools and remote control to solve a large share of encounters. If that is not your preferred style, you do not need to invest heavily in Intelligence just because Cyberpunk is a technology-heavy setting.

A beginner who is curious about netrunning should commit enough points to actually unlock its stronger mechanics rather than splitting Intelligence evenly with four unrelated trees.
contentBlocks.heading: Intelligence — The Core Attribute for Netrunning

contentBlocks.text:
Cool supports stealth-oriented play and other deliberate, precision-focused approaches. It is most useful when you enjoy avoiding direct pressure, controlling when an encounter begins and getting more value from careful positioning.

This can be very effective, but it is slightly less forgiving as a first investment if you are still learning how detection, movement and enemy awareness work. A few survivability or cyberware-focused investments can make the early game more comfortable before Cool becomes your main focus.

Choose it because you enjoy that style, not because you think every character needs points in every attribute.
contentBlocks.heading: Cool — Stealth, Composure and Precision

contentBlocks.text:
A simple first-character plan is to invest enough in Body to feel durable, put meaningful points into Technical Ability for cyberware progression, and then choose one primary identity from Reflexes, Intelligence or Cool.

That produces a character with a stable baseline and one clear specialty instead of five half-developed trees. It also makes perk choices easier because the game presents fewer relevant branches at once.

As you play, let your actual habits guide the next points. If you constantly wish you moved faster, Reflexes is telling you something. If hacking becomes your favorite tool, Intelligence should rise. If you are always trying to avoid detection, Cool deserves more attention.
contentBlocks.heading: A Flexible Beginner Attribute Plan

contentBlocks.text:
Endgame build planners are useful once you understand what the perks mean, but they can make a first playthrough harder to read. A level-by-level template may ask you to invest toward an ability whose purpose will not make sense until much later.

Instead, unlock perks whose benefits you can immediately explain. Movement feels better, cyberware capacity becomes more useful, survivability improves, or a hacking interaction becomes available. That feedback teaches you the system faster than copying a finished build backward.

Because perk points are refundable individually, your early perk choices are experiments rather than permanent mistakes.
contentBlocks.heading: Do Not Copy an Endgame Build Too Early

contentBlocks.text:
Update 2.0 gives existing and new characters a one-time opportunity to fully redistribute attributes. That is much more limited than the perk system, where individual points can be refunded freely outside combat.

Do not use the attribute reset just because one level-up felt inefficient. Save it for a genuine change of direction — for example, when you understand the game well enough to know that the character you built is not the one you want to keep playing.

The best protection against needing it early is simple: concentrate your attribute spending instead of scattering points everywhere.
contentBlocks.heading: Save the One-Time Attribute Reset Until You Really Need It

conclusion:
For a first Cyberpunk 2077 character, Body and Technical Ability are the most forgiving foundations, while Reflexes, Intelligence and Cool are better treated as choices about how you want the character to play. Pick one of those identities and develop it with purpose instead of trying to unlock everything at once.

The modern perk system is designed for experimentation, so refund and rearrange individual perks whenever a choice is not working. Be more deliberate with attribute points, keep the one-time reset in reserve, and let the build grow around the systems you actually enjoy using.
